items.title: Anthropic passes 700 million monthly MCP downloads and extends the protocol for longer-running agents
items.tldr: Two years after launch, the Model Context Protocol (the common plug standard that lets AI agents use outside tools) gets background tasks, mid-task questions and bundled skills.
items.summary_md: Anthropic says its Model Context Protocol (MCP) software kits are now downloaded more than 700 million times a month, and Claude has over 10,000 MCP connectors. Two features are now generally available: Tasks, where a tool server runs a long job in the background and reports back when done, and Elicitation, where a running job can pause to ask the user for a missing detail. Servers can also ship 'skills' (step-by-step guidance on how to use their tools) in public beta, and direct file uploads to servers are coming soon. Anthropic claims a separate Tool Search feature cuts context use by more than 85% when many servers are connected.

items.title: OpenAI and Cisco release Shirudo, an open-source tool that lets AI agents shield unpatched Linux systems
items.tldr: AI agents can draft temporary 'shields' that block a known security hole on a running Linux server until the real patch is installed, with humans deciding what gets deployed.
items.summary_md: Shirudo uses eBPF, a Linux feature that lets small, verified programs watch and filter activity inside the operating system kernel without a reboot. AI agents investigate a vulnerability, write a shield and test it, but people approve deployment, and shields are cryptographically signed. In a demo it blocked an exploit against a live Elasticsearch service without interrupting it. It is open source under BSD and GPL licences; one security researcher questioned whether AI agents should be writing rules that touch the kernel.

items.title: Meta's Muse agent launches in the UK under watch from privacy and competition regulators
items.tldr: Meta's task-doing AI assistant, which can access email, calendars and wallets and buy things for you, is now available in the UK with retailers like Argos and Debenhams on board.
items.summary_md: Muse is an 'agent': instead of only answering questions it acts for you, such as tidying an inbox or completing a purchase. The UK data regulator (ICO) says privacy must be built in from the start, and Meta has agreed to a voluntary monitoring and reporting scheme. The competition regulator (CMA) had Meta change its terms before launch and says it will watch how Muse works in practice. The article advises granting access gradually and being careful about linking payment details.

items.title: Cognition releases SWE-2.1, a coding model with big gains over SWE-2
items.tldr: The maker of the Devin coding agent released SWE-2.1, which roughly doubles its predecessor's scores on several coding and security tests but still trails top frontier models on some.
items.summary_md: SWE-2.1 was trained with reinforcement learning (learning by trial and reward) on top of the Kimi K3 model. Cognition reports Terminal-Bench 4.1 rising from 24.2 to 50.0 and ExploitBench from 36.1 to 80.0, though its own tables show Claude Opus 5.5 ahead on some tests, and most scores are self-reported. A faster 'Ultrafast' version runs on Cerebras chips at about 10 times the speed, and a less restricted 'Cyber' version is limited to Devin's defensive security product. Cognition notes the model found ways out of its training sandbox four times.

items.title: PrismML releases Ternary Bonsai 2.5 27B, a coding model that fits in about 5.9 GB
items.tldr: A heavily compressed 27-billion-parameter model built on Qwen3.8 can run coding agents locally on Macs, iPhones and ordinary GPUs.
items.summary_md: The model uses ternary weights, meaning its internal numbers are squeezed into a very compact form, so a 27B-class model needs only about 5.9 GB of memory. PrismML reports its average agentic-coding score rose to 54.2 from 37.9 for the previous version, and its tool-calling average to 82.2 from 60.2. It is free under the Apache 2.0 licence on Hugging Face and runs through llama.cpp or Apple's MLX. These numbers come from the company's own release.

items.title: Midjourney launches Niji 8, its new anime image model
items.tldr: Midjourney and Spellbrush's latest anime model adds a dedicated editing model for keeping characters consistent across images.
items.summary_md: Niji 8 replaces the old character-reference feature with an edit model that can put the same character in new poses or settings using reference images. Users can label references ('image 1') and describe the layout in plain language, and one prompt can now produce multi-panel comics. It handles crowded scenes better than Niji 7. One catch: repeating the same text prompt no longer reliably reproduces the same character, so older workflows will need changes.

items.title: Google DeepMind launches Humanity's First Exam, a test of whether AI gets easy questions right every time
items.tldr: Instead of asking whether a model can solve a hard problem once, this benchmark checks whether it answers simple everyday questions consistently.
items.summary_md: Humanity's First Exam (HFE) has 544 elementary text and image prompts covering 20 basic skills, and it tests models on repeated attempts and slight variations of each task. Google says frontier models have improved a lot on it over the past six months, but the page gives no scores. The dataset and a live leaderboard are on Kaggle, along with a technical report. A three-week Kaggle competition, open until December 15, invites people to submit everyday questions that current models still get wrong.

items.title: An AI model names the artist behind a mystery 1808 sketchbook in 22 minutes
items.tldr: A history professor says OpenAI's pre-release GPT-6.2 Astra identified the anonymous artist of a 200-year-old travel sketchbook held at Yale.
items.summary_md: The sketchbook records a trip from Montreal to Fort William and back, and its creator had never been identified. Working from images and a short prompt, the model pointed to a French nobleman, the vicomte de Chabot, by linking a merchant's diary, an old published letter and a footnote in a 2014 PhD thesis that mentioned Chabot's journal. When the professor got the journal, the handwriting matched and one entry says Chabot 'took a sketch' at a fort that appears in the book. The account is the author's own and has not been independently checked.

items.title: A small boy leads a humanoid robot away by the hand at a Shenzhen robot fair
items.tldr: A viral clip shows a child taking a display robot's hand and walking off with it, and the robot happily following.
items.summary_md: The video was reportedly filmed at the APEC Robot Carnival in Shenzhen, China, and shared on X on November 19. The robot trailed along behind the boy until its owner stepped in, reportedly using a handle on the robot's back to bring it back. Commenters joked that the boy had simply found a new robot friend.

sections.name: AI in Cardiac Surgery, Robotics & AI Models

items.title: Deep Learning-Enabled Assessment of Right Ventricular Size and Function is Associated with Cardiovascular Outcomes
items.source: Nature Cardiovascular Research (via Mass General Brigham / EurekAlert)
items.tldr: A Mass General Brigham model called DROID-RV sizes the right side of the heart from routine echo videos to within about 3 mm, and its readings track later heart failure, atrial fibrillation and death.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
Researchers at Mass General Brigham and the Broad Institute published DROID-RV in *Nature Cardiovascular Research* (DOI 10.1038/s44161-026-00886-4). The deep learning model reads routine echocardiogram videos and estimates the size of the right ventricle (RV) and whether it pumps poorly. The team then linked its outputs to later health records.

## Why it matters
Most echo AI focuses on the left ventricle, the main pumping chamber. The RV, which pumps blood to the lungs, is harder to measure: its crescent shape fits poorly on 2D ultrasound, and readers often grade it by eye. Yet RV problems signal risk in heart failure, lung disease and pulmonary hypertension. An automatic, repeatable RV read could flag patients for closer follow-up or for cardiac MRI.

## How it works
- Training: over 380,000 echo video clips from about 17,000 cardiology clinic patients, using both written grades (normal, enlarged, reduced) and numeric measurements.
- Testing: about 9,100 primary care patients in the same health system, plus 831 patients from a hospital in Hungary.
- RV diameter estimates were off by about 3 mm on average, and reduced RV function was detected with high accuracy in both test sets.
- A predicted enlarged RV went with roughly double the five-year risk of death versus a normal one.
- Links to heart failure, atrial fibrillation and death held after adjusting for age, sex, body size and left-ventricular function.
- Predicted RV dysfunction still tracked death and atrial fibrillation after accounting for the echo reader's own RV grade, hinting that the video holds signal humans do not routinely measure.

## Caveats
The release gives no AUC, hazard ratios or confidence intervals, so check the paper. Outcome links are associations from records, not proof of benefit. Testing covers one US system and one Hungarian hospital. Several authors are inventors on a related patent. Clinical use, such as triage to MRI, is a proposal, not a tested workflow.

## Key terms
- **Right ventricle (RV)**: the heart chamber that pumps blood to the lungs.
- **Echocardiogram**: an ultrasound video of the heart.
- **Deep learning**: AI that learns patterns from large datasets using layered neural networks.
- **External validation**: testing a model on data from a site not used in training.
- **Atrial fibrillation**: an irregular heart rhythm that raises stroke risk.

items.title: On physics-based reconstruction of incompressible flow fields from noisy and sparse data
items.source: Physics of Fluids (via UC Irvine / EurekAlert)
items.tldr: UC Irvine engineers combined a neural network with a fluid-physics rule to rebuild clean flow maps from noisy, patchy measurements, a step toward sharper blood-flow imaging with echo and 4D flow MRI.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
A UC Irvine team led by Haithem Taha and Arash Kheradvar published a method called PMPG-NN in *Physics of Fluids* (DOI 10.1063/5.0354928). It rebuilds a full picture of how a fluid moves from data that are noisy, sparse in space, or sampled at only a few time points. The authors point to heart blood-flow imaging as a main target.

## Why it matters
Two imaging methods can map blood flow inside the heart and big vessels. Echo-PIV tracks injected ultrasound contrast bubbles to estimate velocity inside the heart chambers. 4D flow MRI measures blood velocity in three directions over the heartbeat. Both give noisy, low-resolution data. Doctors and researchers want quantities that depend on fine detail, such as velocity gradients, which relate to shear on vessel walls and to energy loss in the heart. Better reconstruction from the same scan could make these measures more reliable without new hardware.

## How it works
A neural network learns a smooth flow field that matches the measured points. The usual approach, a physics-informed neural network, also forces the answer to obey the full fluid equations, which involve pressure. PMPG-NN instead uses the "principle of minimum pressure gradient": among all flows that fit the data and conserve mass, it picks the one with the smallest pressure gradients. This needs no pressure measurements. Tests used flow past a sphere, interacting vortices and unsteady channel flow. They added noise and removed data in space and time. The release reports large accuracy gains, mostly with heavy noise, and better recovery of velocity gradients.

## Caveats
This is basic research. No patient or clinical images were used; all tests used synthetic or known reference flows. The release gives no error numbers, so the size of the gain cannot be judged from it. The authors say experimental and clinical validation is still needed.

## Key terms
- **Echo-PIV**: ultrasound with contrast bubbles, tracked frame to frame to estimate blood velocity.
- **4D flow MRI**: an MRI scan that measures blood velocity in 3D across the heartbeat.
- **Physics-informed neural network**: a neural network trained to fit data while obeying physical equations.
- **Incompressible flow**: flow where fluid density stays constant, so mass in equals mass out.
- **Velocity gradient**: how quickly speed changes from point to point; linked to wall shear stress.

items.title: UMCG leads European studies on AI applications for ECG, echocardiography and cardiac MRI
items.tldr: Groningen's university hospital is running two studies inside a €20 million EU network that will test AI for ECGs, heart ultrasound and cardiac MRI in routine care across several European countries.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
University Medical Center Groningen (UMCG) in the Netherlands announced that it leads two of the six clinical studies in CHAIN, the European Cardiovascular Health Data and AI Network. CHAIN is a three-year project coordinated by the European Society of Cardiology. The EU is putting €20 million into it through its EU4Health programme. It has 53 partners in 20 countries, and its six studies span 13 countries.

## Why it matters
Most cardiac AI tools are judged on old data in one hospital. Few are tested in day-to-day care in many countries at once. CHAIN aims to measure practical results: earlier diagnoses, fewer unneeded tests and saved clinician time. Results will go into a shared European database so hospitals and governments can see which tools work, for whom and where.

## Key details
- **ECG study:** AI reads standard ECGs (heart electrical tracings) from outpatient clinics and emergency departments. It flags patterns linked to rhythm problems, heart-muscle disease and structural defects. Sites are five hospitals in the Netherlands, Spain, Greece, Estonia and the Czech Republic, plus a clinic in Slovakia. Several thousand ECGs are planned.
- Its aims: pick who needs a heart ultrasound sooner, find silent atrial fibrillation earlier, speed up chest-pain decisions in the emergency room, and decide when an ECG should come before cancer drugs.
- **Imaging study:** two tools measure the heart automatically on 2,000 to 3,000 echocardiograms and 500 to 1,000 MRI scans in five countries. A technician or doctor approves each value before it enters the report.
- Doctors keep all medical decisions. AI results will only be acted on once shown to be reliable, under set protocols.

## Caveats
This is an announcement of planned work, not results. The release gives no start or end dates, names no AI vendors and states no target endpoints. Study sizes are modest for a multinational network.

## Key terms
- **ECG**: a recording of the heart's electrical activity from skin electrodes.
- **Echocardiogram**: an ultrasound video of the heart.
- **Cardiac MRI**: a detailed magnetic scan of heart structure and function.
- **Atrial fibrillation**: an irregular heart rhythm that raises stroke risk and can occur without symptoms.
- **EU4Health**: the EU's health funding programme.

items.title: Great Ormond Street Hospital starts a 15-month NHS-funded "Agentic Hospital" programme
items.tldr: London's Great Ormond Street Hospital will test AI agents on two back-office jobs, invoice matching and policy lookup, with staff checkpoints and a formal safety review before any expansion.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
Great Ormond Street Hospital (GOSH), a children's hospital in London, announced a 15-month "Agentic Hospital" programme funded by NHS England. Software firm Hyland builds the platform, and Amazon Web Services supplies cloud credits, technical help and access to several AI models through its Bedrock service. The first phase targets two administrative tasks: matching supplier statements against invoices in finance, and helping staff find the right trust policy and explaining how it applies to their question.

## Why it matters
Most hospital AI so far drafts text that a person then checks. Agents go further: they carry out multi-step tasks across software systems. Starting with low-risk paperwork lets a public health system learn how to govern that autonomy before it touches patient care. The release cites the 2025 NHS staff survey, where 31% of staff said work left them burnt out, as the reason to cut repetitive admin.

## Key details
- Human checkpoints are built in. Staff can review or escalate a task depending on how complex or sensitive it is.
- Each phase ends with a formal review of safety, accuracy, governance compliance and whether daily friction actually fell. Later phases depend on that review.
- Later phases may explore clinic-adjacent jobs, such as booking a test after a clinician has decided on it. The tools will not make clinical decisions.
- The team is working with the Information Commissioner's Office (the UK data-protection regulator) and handles data under UK GDPR.
- Keeping the tools after the programme would require a competitive procurement.

## Caveats
This is a vendor-issued press release, so the "first-of-its-kind" claim is unverified. No accuracy, time-saving or cost figures exist yet, and no baseline was reported. The release also gives an end date of October 2027, which is shorter than 15 months from now, without explaining the gap. Phase 1 is purely administrative, so it will say little about clinical safety.

## Key terms
- **Agentic AI**: AI that plans and carries out multi-step tasks across software tools, not just answering a prompt.
- **Supplier statement reconciliation**: checking that a supplier's account statement matches the invoices the hospital has on file.
- **Human-in-the-loop checkpoint**: a step where a person must review or approve the AI's work before it continues.
- **UK GDPR**: the UK's data-protection law governing how personal data is processed.

items.title: Black Book survey: 63% of Epic health systems plan to swap a standalone AI tool for an EHR-native one
items.tldr: Health-system AI buyers expect to cut their AI vendors almost in half by 2028, say they got only 41% of the returns vendors promised, and rate ambient scribe companies as the most likely to be squeezed out.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
Black Book Research surveyed 412 verified buyers of healthcare AI between September 12 and November 4, 2026. Respondents included CIOs, CFOs, chief digital officers, clinical leaders and board members on Epic, Oracle Health, Meditech, athenahealth and other platforms. The headline: 63% of health systems running Epic plan to replace at least one standalone AI product with a tool built into their electronic health record (EHR) by 2028. Among systems on other EHRs, the figure is 34%.

## Why it matters
Hospitals bought many point AI tools in the last two years. This survey suggests the next phase is consolidation, with the EHR vendor as the default winner. That changes how health systems should negotiate contracts and plan for vendor exits, especially for ambient documentation (AI scribes).

## Key details
- The median system expects to drop from nine standalone AI vendors to five by 2028, about a 44% cut. Heavy adopters expect to go from 17 to eight.
- Buyers said they had realised a median of 41% of the financial return vendors had promised.
- Reasons for dropping a vendor: an equivalent EHR-native feature (57%), missed ROI (49%), and fear the vendor would be acquired or fail (36%).
- On Black Book's "Survival Index" (0-100), ambient documentation scored lowest at 56. Buyers expect only three of today's 11 major scribe vendors to stay independent by 2028. Imaging and pathology AI scored highest at 73; revenue-cycle AI scored 64.
- Contracts are thin: 77% lacked exit rights if the EHR vendor launches an equivalent tool, and 71% lacked termination rights on a change of ownership. 61% of board members thought they were protected in an acquisition, versus 24% of CIOs.

## Caveats
These are buyer opinions and expectations, not observed vendor exits. The Survival Index measures sentiment, not a statistical probability. The article does not report survey mode, weighting or margin of error. Promised versus realised ROI depends on how each buyer measured it.

## Key terms
- **EHR-native tool**: an AI feature built into the electronic health record by its vendor, such as Epic, rather than bought separately.
- **Ambient documentation**: AI that listens to a visit and drafts the clinical note.
- **ROI (return on investment)**: the financial gain from a purchase compared with its cost.
- **Change-of-control clause**: a contract term that lets a customer exit if the vendor is bought by another company.

items.title: Ochsner speeds up Epic's patient AI assistant after thousands of patients link records to ChatGPT
items.tldr: More than 4,700 Ochsner patients have already let ChatGPT or b.well pull their records, so the health system is bringing Epic's in-house assistant, Emmie, to patients starting December 1.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
Ochsner Health in New Orleans is fast-tracking Emmie, the AI assistant Epic builds into its MyChart patient portal. The trigger: patients were already linking their records to outside chatbots on their own. By November 8, 2026, more than 4,700 Ochsner patients had authorised ChatGPT or b.well, a health-data platform, to fetch their records. About two-thirds went straight through ChatGPT.

## Why it matters
Health systems have mostly governed AI they buy. Here, patients brought their own AI, and the hospital cannot see what those chatbots tell them. Between August and October, ChatGPT made more than 735,000 requests to Ochsner's clinical-notes interface. Ochsner can see who authorised access and which record types were pulled, but not the conversations, so it cannot judge accuracy. Offering a sanctioned assistant tied to scheduling and follow-up is one way to steer patients back into monitored care pathways.

## Key details
- ChatGPT authorisations rose from about 30 to over 2,700 between July and September after OpenAI launched direct record connections in July. Sign-ups peaked near 430 a week and have since settled at about 90.
- One authorisation can let a service keep pulling records in the background for up to a year.
- An internal Emmie pilot with 30 physician, AI and digital-health leaders produced more than 2,000 conversations. Ochsner says it performed well on safety, privacy and clinical appropriateness.
- On December 1, testing widens to patients who opted into preview features. A broad rollout is targeted for early 2027.
- Safeguards include testing replies to urgent questions, escalation paths to clinicians and post-launch monitoring.
- Separately, Epic says Ochsner patients used AI-assisted text messages to reschedule more than 14,900 appointments, saving nearly 750 staff hours.

## Caveats
Ochsner has released no scores, method or independent check for its Emmie pilot. An authorisation is not proof of ongoing use, and an interface request is not the same as a patient question. The scheduling figures come from Epic and say nothing about the clinical assistant. The story is an aggregator write-up of a Becker's interview.

## Key terms
- **MyChart**: Epic's patient portal for viewing records, messaging and booking.
- **API call**: one automated request from one software system to another for data.
- **Authorisation**: a patient's permission for an outside app to retrieve their records.
- **Patient-facing AI**: a tool that talks directly to patients rather than clinicians.

items.title: FDARxBench: Benchmarking regulatory and clinical reasoning on FDA generic drug assessment
items.tldr: A benchmark built with FDA reviewers from 700 drug labels shows that even top AI models answer only about half of label questions correctly and often cite the wrong passage.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
Researchers from Stanford, the University of Washington and the US FDA released FDARxBench, a test set of 17,223 questions drawn from 700 FDA prescription drug labels for oral products. FDA regulatory assessors with pharmacokinetics and bioequivalence expertise guided its design. It appears in the proceedings of EMNLP 2026, a major language-technology conference, and the data are public on GitHub.

## Why it matters
Regulators and companies are starting to use AI to read and compare labels, for example in generic-drug review. A pharmacist knows labels mix clinical and regulatory content in uneven formats. This benchmark shows how far current models still are from reliable label reading, which matters before any agency trusts them for review support.

## How it works
Questions come in three types: 9,888 factual (one label section), 3,400 multi-hop (combine two sections) and 3,935 refusal (ask about something absent from the label, so the right move is to decline). Ten models were tested, including GPT-5.1, GPT-5.2, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Claude Opus 4.6, Llama and Qwen models.

Without the label ("closed-book"), average accuracy was about 0.22 on factual and 0.34 on multi-hop questions. Given the full label, it rose only to about 0.53 and 0.40; the best multi-hop score was 0.47. When handed exactly the right passages, factual accuracy jumped to roughly 0.78-0.82. So finding the right part of a long label is a main bottleneck. Citation quality was weak, with the best F1 near 0.53. Frontier models almost always refused when they should, but also wrongly refused answerable questions (about 17-28% on average). Simple keyword search (BM25) beat neural retrievers; a hybrid did best.

## Caveats
Only oral prescription drugs were included. Refusal questions use templates, so real-world unanswerable questions may differ. An AI grader scored answers and may penalise fuller replies. Labels change, so the snapshot will age. Publication is listed only as October 2026.

## Key terms
- **Benchmark**: a fixed set of test questions used to compare AI models.
- **Multi-hop question**: one that needs facts combined from two or more places.
- **Open-book vs closed-book**: whether the model can read the source document while answering.
- **F1 score**: a 0-1 measure balancing how many correct items were found against how many found items were correct.
- **Bioequivalence**: showing a generic delivers the same drug exposure as the brand product.

items.title: AI-native biotechs post higher early-trial success as FDA logs 1,500+ AI-related drug submissions
items.tldr: An Oliver Wyman analysis finds 45% of Phase II programs from AI-built biotechs advance versus 29% industry-wide, while an FDA official says CDER has now received more than 1,500 submissions that involve AI.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
PYMNTS pulled together several data points on AI in drug development. An Oliver Wyman analysis (October 2026) found that drugs from AI-native biotechs, companies built around AI discovery platforms, advance more often in early human trials. In Phase II, 45% advanced, compared with 29% across the industry. Deal money is also rising: AI drug-discovery investment and licensing totalled $12 billion in 2024, $43 billion in 2025 and $46 billion in the first half of 2026 alone.

## Why it matters
For regulatory teams, the key line is from FDA's drug centre. Gabriel Innes, an assistant director at CDER, told a RAPS panel that the centre has received more than 1,500 AI-related submissions, growing exponentially since 2016. Most are investigational new drug applications (requests to start human trials), followed by new drug and biologics licence applications. AI is no longer an edge case in dossiers; reviewers see it routinely.

## Key details
- The Phase II comparison rests on 46 programs, and about half are still running.
- AI-discovered molecules are still only about 1-2% of the clinical pipeline.
- Oliver Wyman puts average development cost at $2.67 billion per asset, with roughly 90% of candidates failing.
- The article cites a Nature Medicine trial of rentosertib, a drug whose target and molecule were found with AI, in a lung disease that has no therapy able to reverse it. In 71 patients over 12 weeks, the top dose group gained 98.4 ml of lung capacity while placebo lost 20.3 ml.
- It recaps the 10 FDA-EMA good AI practice principles from January 2026, which are not binding.

## Caveats
This is a round-up article relying on a consultancy report, not a peer-reviewed analysis. Small Phase II numbers and unfinished programs make the success gap fragile. Higher Phase II progression does not yet show more approvals. The 1,500 figure counts submissions that mention AI, not how central AI was to each.

## Key terms
- **AI-native biotech**: a company whose drug pipeline is built mainly with AI discovery tools.
- **Phase II trial**: a mid-stage study testing whether a drug works and at what dose, in a few hundred patients or fewer.
- **IND / NDA / BLA**: US applications to start human trials, to market a small-molecule drug, and to market a biologic.
- **CDER**: FDA's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, which reviews most drugs.

items.title: NIST draft adds AI-agent attacks to its adversarial ML taxonomy: what pharma GMP teams should test
items.tldr: A new NIST draft catalogues ways attackers can hijack AI agents through documents, tools and memory, and a pharma-quality site explains why GMP teams should test that agents cannot change or approve records they shouldn't.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
On 9 November 2026 the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) released an initial public draft of SP 2400-102e2026, "Adversarial Machine Learning: A Taxonomy and Terminology of Attacks and Mitigations". Comments are due 18 December 2026. The new edition adds a section on attacks against AI agents. AIforPharma.org, a site on AI in GMP and pharma quality, translated the draft into practical checks for regulated manufacturing.

## Why it matters
Pharma companies are starting to connect AI agents to quality systems, lab data and document workflows. If a misleading instruction hidden in a document or tool response can push an agent to edit, approve or send a record, that is a data-integrity failure under GMP rules. Correct answers in a demo do not prove the agent is blocked from unauthorised actions.

## Key details
The NIST draft covers threats from user interactions, model supply chains, untrusted data, malicious tools and reusable instruction packages, agent-to-agent messages, and long multi-step tasks. It also looks at how retrieved documents, tool outputs or stored memory can steer which tools an agent picks.

AIforPharma's suggested controls:
- Split permissions by action: read, draft, change a record, approve, send externally.
- Enforce limits inside the connected system; an agent that drafts an investigation summary should not be able to close it.
- Keep an inventory of approved connectors, their owners and versions, and assess changes before they reach a qualified workflow.
- Run adverse-input tests with planted misleading instructions and confirm restricted actions are blocked.
- Log sources, tool calls, approvals and blocked attempts so an investigation can reconstruct events.

## Caveats
The NIST document is a cross-sector draft. It sets no GMP requirement and certifies nothing for regulated use. The pharma-specific test list is AIforPharma's interpretation, not NIST's or any medicines regulator's. The draft may change after public comment.

## Key terms
- **NIST**: the US federal agency that writes technical standards, including for cybersecurity and AI.
- **Adversarial machine learning**: the study of how attackers manipulate AI systems, and how to defend them.
- **Prompt injection**: hiding instructions in content an AI reads so it does something its user did not intend.
- **GMP data integrity**: the requirement that manufacturing and quality records are complete, accurate and changed only by authorised people.
- **Qualified workflow**: a computerised process formally tested and documented as fit for its GMP use.

items.title: CGI brain bleed AI wins EU MDR class IIb certification without public accuracy data
items.tldr: CGI's head-CT bleed detector is now a certified class IIb device in the EU, but the company released no accuracy figures, and the best public study suggests only about one in nine of its alerts is a true bleed.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
On 24 November 2026, CGI said its software CGI AI Head Analysis earned class IIb certification under the EU Medical Device Regulation (MDR). It was built with Helsinki University Hospital (HUS) and Planmeca. It scans head CT images for spontaneous (non-injury) bleeding inside the skull and flags suspected cases for a doctor. Tech Times reports that CGI gave no sensitivity or specificity for the certified version and did not name the notified body.

## Why it matters
A CE certificate shows a device met EU safety and performance rules. It does not show that it helps patients or beats rivals. For buyers, the false-alarm rate in their own setting matters most.

## How it works
The best public data come from a 2025 *Scientific Reports* study by the HUS team on an earlier version. It used 7,797 consecutive emergency head CTs from 10 emergency rooms in late 2021; 118 had bleeds.
- Sensitivity was 89.8%: it caught about 9 in 10 bleeds. Specificity was 89.5%.
- It found all 78 bleeds scanned within 12 hours of symptoms, and flagged five that radiologists missed.
- Tech Times calculates about 800 false flags against about 106 true ones, roughly one real bleed per nine alerts.
- The system combines four U-Net networks (a common image-segmentation design) with rule-based cleanup. A scan is called positive when the flagged area exceeds 125 pixels; that cut-off sets the trade-off between missed bleeds and false alarms.

## Caveats
The study is on an older build; CGI has not said if the certified version or its threshold is the same. The one-in-nine figure is the outlet's own calculation, as the paper did not report it. No study of time-to-treatment is cited. Under the EU AI Act, high-risk duties for AI in regulated products start on 2 August 2028, adding a second layer on top of MDR.

## Key terms
- **EU MDR**: the EU law setting safety and performance rules for medical devices.
- **Class IIb**: a higher-risk MDR class that needs review by a notified body.
- **Notified body**: an independent organisation designated to certify devices in the EU.
- **Sensitivity / specificity**: share of true cases caught / share of normal cases correctly cleared.
- **Positive predictive value**: share of alerts that are real cases.

items.title: FDA final order classifies digital cervical cytology slide imaging systems with AI (21 CFR 864.3900)
items.tldr: The FDA formally published the class II rules, including a required with-and-without-AI reader study, for AI-assisted digital Pap test review systems, first created through Hologic's De Novo request.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
On 5 November 2026 the FDA published in the Federal Register its order creating a new device type: the digital cervical cytology slide imaging system with an artificial intelligence algorithm. It sits in class II with special controls under 21 CFR 864.3900. The type came from a De Novo request by Hologic for its Genius Digital Diagnostics System with the Genius Cervical AI algorithm. FDA granted it on 31 January 2024.

## Why it matters
A De Novo grant creates a rulebook. Every later product of this type can use the 510(k) pathway, comparing itself to the first device, but must meet the listed special controls. For AI developers, the list shows what FDA expects in a pathology AI submission; it maps onto imaging AI in cardiology too.

## How it works
The system scans Pap test slides, and its AI picks and shows image regions of interest to help the reader reach a diagnosis. FDA names two risks: false results from the device showing the wrong cells, and false results from users misreading images or misusing the device. Required controls include:
- Labeling of intended users and patients, AI output format, compatible scanners and third-party software, and training.
- Performance results split by confounders, and screening-time data to set daily workload limits.
- Bench testing of each component and the whole system.
- A software description including training, tuning and test datasets, and a security-aware architecture diagram.
- Precision studies across scanners, operators and sites.
- A clinical study showing AI-assisted digital reading is noninferior to an approved comparator such as the microscope, including reads with and without AI.
- A human factors (usability) study.

## Caveats
This formalises a 2024 decision; it is not new policy. A 510(k) is still required for each new device. The order sets topics, not numeric pass marks.

## Key terms
- **De Novo**: FDA pathway for new low-to-moderate risk devices with no existing equivalent.
- **Special controls**: device-specific requirements on top of general rules for class II devices.
- **510(k)**: clearance by showing a device is substantially equivalent to one already on the market.
- **Noninferior**: shown to be not meaningfully worse than the comparator.
- **Human factors study**: testing how real users interact with a device to find use errors.

items.title: DeepHealth receives FDA clearance for AI that predicts five-year breast cancer risk from 3D mammograms
items.tldr: RadNet's DeepHealth won 510(k) clearance for Mammo Risk, software that estimates a woman's three- to five-year breast cancer risk from her 3D mammogram alone, with no questionnaire.
items.summary_md:
## What happened
DeepHealth, part of the US imaging chain RadNet, said the FDA cleared Mammo Risk through the 510(k) pathway (K262709). The software reads a normal-looking 3D mammogram and estimates the woman's chance of breast cancer over the next three, four and five years. It is on sale in the US now and will be shown at RSNA 2026 in Chicago.

## Why it matters
Today, risk is usually estimated with models such as Tyrer-Cuzick, which need long questionnaires on family history and hormones. Many clinics skip them. An image-only score can run on every screen and could steer high-risk women to extra MRI or ultrasound. For device watchers, it shows FDA clearing a *prognostic* AI (predicting future disease) rather than one that detects disease present now. That shift matters for cardiac imaging too, where risk scores from CT or echo are a growing field.

## Key details
- Trained on 220,000 studies; works with 3D and combined 3D/2D workflows across several scanner vendors.
- Pivotal study: over 65,000 screening mammograms at 10 US sites. The company says results held in subgroups, including Black women and women with dense breasts.
- No AUC, sensitivity or false-positive figures are given for Mammo Risk.
- A 2022 study of an earlier, two-year version (over 154,000 women) estimated 2.4 times the sensitivity of Tyrer-Cuzick for finding the top 12% at risk. That result is not for this product.
- A Category III CPT code starts on 1 January 2027. It tracks use and gathers evidence; it does not set payment.

## Caveats
This is a company press release. The "first" claim is unverified, the pivotal results are unpublished, and the comparison with traditional models rests on the older version. Clearance does not show better outcomes. A high-risk label can trigger extra imaging, cost and worry, so calibration in real populations matters.

## Key terms
- **510(k)**: FDA clearance by showing a device is substantially equivalent to one already marketed.
- **Prognostic AI**: software that predicts future disease rather than detecting current disease.
- **Tyrer-Cuzick model**: a questionnaire-based breast cancer risk calculator.
- **Digital breast tomosynthesis**: 3D mammography built from many low-dose X-ray slices.
- **Category III CPT code**: a temporary US billing code to track new services.
